newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: W. Australia gold royalty said to cause net loss.
newsitem.headline: W. Australia gold royalty said to cause net loss.

text.p: Western Australia would lose A$500 million a year in gold production and investment in the industry would be cut by A$200 million if the state government introduced a 2.5 percent gold royalty, the Association of Mining and Exploration Companies (AMEC) said on Wednesday.

AMEC said this in reporting results of a representative industry survey, covering nine mines across the state with forecast production life of 260 tonnes of gold, with 10 percent of the gold industry work force.
The survey also indicated there would be an average reduction in mine lives of one year, it said in a statement.
The survey formed part of a background paper prepared by economic consultants ACiL Pty Ltd and released by AMEC.
Gold was the most valuable mineral commodity produced in Western Australia and employed the largest proportion of the resource sector work force, AMEC said.

The paper said that while the proposed royalty would raise about A$70 million-A$90 million a year, this would be offset by reduced production, payroll tax, stamp duties and other taxes and charges paid by gold producers and their suppliers.

A study by the University of Western Australia suggested that a 2.5 percent royalty would reduce gold production by the same amount, reduce gross domestic product by A$370 million and produce an associated income loss for the state of A$250 million, AMEC said.
The royalty would reduce earnings per share in mining companies by an average of eight percent with an average reduction in company valuations of 2.4 percent, it said.
Hardest hit would be companies with all their operations in Western Australia, it said.
The gold sector occupied a special place in Western Australia and should be treated differently, AMEC executive officer economics, Adrienne Wright, said in the statement.

State Premier Richard Court has proposed introducing a royalty of 1.25 percent of gold sale proceeds from January 1 next year, rising to 2.5 percent by July 1999, to compensate for cuts in Federal funding to the state.
